newsitem.title: LAOS: Laos dismisses foreign fears on economic reform.
newsitem.headline: Laos dismisses foreign fears on economic reform.

text.p: Communist Laos has dismissed foreign concerns about the direction of its economy and vowed to implement more economic reforms despite leadership changes earlier this year.

Finance Minister Saysomphone Phomvihane told Reuters in an interview that the government had maintained high economic growth in the 1996 fiscal year ending September 30, while also managing to scale down inflation growth.
"The economic development in (fiscal) 1996 has been on a good track which shows in the figures of high GDP (gross domestic product) growth of 7.1 percent," he said in an interview late on Thursday.
The tiny, impoverished and land-locked Laos with 4.5 million inhabitants has an annual per capita income of US$350.

The Lao Revolutionary People's Revolutionary Party which took power in 1975 has been steering the nation towards economic modernisation along the same lines as Vietnam, foreign economic analysts said.

The economy slipped to near-collapse in the mid-1980s after which the government introduced market-style reforms. The new policies were further developed in the 1990s, prompted by the loss of backing and aid from Moscow.
At a key party congress in March, officials projected average annual GDP growth of 8.5 percent for the next five years. Yearly growth in 1991-95 averaged 6.4 percent.
United Nations figures estimate the economy grew by 7.1 percent in 1995.

It was at that party congress that deputy premier and politburo member Khamphoui Keoboualapha, who had spearheaded economic reforms, was dropped from both the politburo and the party's 49-member central committee.
Foreign observers had speculated then that the change might slow reform but Saysomphone said progress towards improving the economy had been steady.

"Another good result is that the inflation rate has been reduced. Compared to the end of 1995 where the average was about 19 percent, now inflation is about 12 percent," Saysomphone said. "In addition to that the revenue side has also been increased."

Earlier this year the government projected 16 percent inflation growth for fiscal 1996. Revenue for the national budget rose five percent from the original target of 220 billion kip ($564 million), he said.

Saysomphone said the decline in inflation growth was due to a range of monetary measures implemented this year including introduction of a new legal framework for taxes and a credit control programme.
He said the government was dedicated to continued economic liberalisation and reforms and did not want to see any economic slowdown.
"In fact, the policy won't change and we stress we will strictly implement economic reform and move towards a full market economy," he said.
Saysomphone projects continued GDP growth in the coming fiscal year, to about 7.5 percent. Inflation should drop further to about 10 percent.
Laos's high 1995 inflation, which came on the heels of single-digit price rises from 1992-94, was attributed partly to fiscal expansion designed to bolster market reforms, experts have said.
With guidance from the International Monetary Fund and U.N. agencies, Laos is trying to get inflation under control and deal with problems caused by a softening of its currency.
"The exchange rate has remained quite stable at about 900 kip per U.S. dollar. The gap between the official exchange rate and parallel market remains low at about one to two percent."
